new possibility for calculating critical properties of high-charge operators $\phi^Q$, where the charge $Q$ is fixed. For operators of a given charge, the mathematical structure of their critical properties can be discovered by examining the solution to a modified version of the nonlinear $\phi^4$ field theory in the vicinity of the Gaussian fixed point, with the exception of one unique operator whose properties exhibit an irregular renormalization behavior. The peculiar renormalization properties of an operator of a specific charge are a consequence of its symmetry properties. The operators whose charge is an even integer divided by 2 possess an $O((Q/2)^{2}\ln Q)$ component in their renormalization, while those with an odd integer charge of 1 have a finite renormalization effect. The large-charge expansion can be used together with other theoretical methods, such as the perturbation theory in the vicinity of the IR fixed point or the perturbative Ginzburg-Landau theory, in order to calculate critical properties. At a high enough value of $Q$, there will be a threshold beyond which the effects of both the Gaussian and IR renormalization become equally dominant in determining the contribution to the free-energy density. The effects of both scenarios start to align as the charge continues to rise. The large-charge expansion could potentially be used to calculate the critical properties of operators with an even greater charge than what perturbative Ginzburg-Landau theory can handle.

It is noted that in certain cases, binary power control can lead to nearly maximal interference while optimal power control delivers significantly higher loads, also demonstrating that extremal gain values can serve as a performance metric for network design. Additionally, this research proposes new metrics for measuring load improvement and network efficiency, also providing their corresponding connections to GDoF analyses. Numerical studies have shown that in some cases, binary power control can achieve near maximal network efficiency while also delivering high loads. It is noted that: 1) an additional 50% load increase from optimal (extremal) power control to binary power control can be considered high load; 2) an 89% increase is considered large load; and 3) a 100% increase is considered double load. Also, this research has connected these new metrics to GDoF analyses, thus making them relevant from a theoretical perspective.

Before initiating the fine-tuning of BERT, we employ a deep neural network to refine the resulting text embeddings while minimizing the number of categories. This two-stage method, which utilizes two hyper-networks, is a key aspect of our proposed system. To further increase the model's efficiency, we have also implemented a sparse output layer, which reduces the model's parameters and thus its complexity. Finally, to verify the efficacy of our proposed model, we conducted an experiment on a large dataset of unstructured text in the financial sector, yielding an impressive F1-score of 0.79 across 41 distinct audit findings categories. This result represents a significant advancement over the current state-of-the-art models in this domain.

This led to a refined entanglement entropy, which can be represented by a modified logarithmic function, incorporating a constant term along with a dipole term governed by the momentum's divergence. This enhanced understanding of entanglement, when applied to black holes, results in a revised temperature definition. Specifically, for rotating and charged black holes, their temperatures are now a constant value, rather than proportional to the horizon's angular velocity and electrical charge. Furthermore, this refined theory enables the resolution of the holographic information paradox, as the black hole's surface having a finite radius effectively eliminates the ultraviolet divergences associated with the entanglement entropy, rendering the information paradox resolvable.

is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. This breakthrough enables the possibility of applying this control strategy to larger robots moving on densely packed granular surfaces that closely resemble solid terrain.

(IoT) networks, periodic firmware updates are vital for maintaining optimal security and efficiency. Given the trend towards edge-based computing, these updates should ideally minimize the latency until which normal service can be restored. Although partial firmware updates have been explored in related fields, such as computing systems and networks, their feasibility for IoT devices has yet to be investigated. The unique limitations and opportunities presented by these devices offer an exciting opportunity for applying lessons learned in more complex systems. Our study focuses on designing efficient, near-optimal partial firmware updates for IoT devices, which often feature binary firmware. By comparing different strategies like topological support enumeration and iterative methods with single-point optimization, we identify and demonstrate the superior approach, which also yields an associated quality of service metric. Furthermore, we illustrate the main challenges encountered in implementing this approach and discuss potential optimizations. Finally, we use linear programming to prove the optimality of the proposed method and develop an associated polyhedral guarantee for finding optimal solutions, which can be computed efficiently using the Chv\'{a}tal-Gomory method.

Our results show that the local self-energy's imaginary component, which governs the decay rate of initially localized states, can serve as a probabilistic phase transition order parameter, facilitating the characterization of critical behavior and multifractal nature in many-body localized states across various disorder intensities. Moreover, we establish that the fractal dimension associated with the local self-energy experiences a discontinuous change at the phase transition, where it transitions from less than one in the localized phase to one in the thermal phase. Furthermore, the local self-energy's asymptotic scaling behavior in the vicinity of the critical disorder strength is non-uniform, featuring an essential singularity due to a non-ergodic volume, which remains finite at criticality. Our findings are further validated through the verification of self-energy's expected renormalization in the many-body localized phase across multiple disorder intensities.

interactive graph search groups specific labels in a structured framework that benefits image recognition, product organization, and database retrieval. However, current research mainly focuses on finding a single optimal label at a time and encounters two primary challenges - it often requires an excessive amount of questions and fails to tackle multiple targets efficiently. In response to these obstacles, this study introduces the kBM-IGS problem, where we must determine a k-sized set of selections with minimal distance to given targets while adhering to a predetermined budget of questions. The BM part represents that selections are chosen to best match the targets, and this is distinct from prior studies that often involve penalizing suboptimal choices. We develop three novel algorithms - one is a simulation model that establishes the optimal connection between set size and query count, and the other two are practical methods based on these findings to address the BM-IGS issue with improved efficiency. These algorithms are then integrated to address the kBM-IGS problem, and our empirical data demonstrates that they can successfully tackle 10 targets while other methods struggle with 1.

This breakthrough reveals that when subjected to these high-frequency sound waves, colloidal gels exhibit a profound reduction in rigidity. Currently, classification primarily relies on human expertise, but semi-supervised Machine Learning algorithms can aid this process by utilizing labeled data to predict subject classes for previously uncategorized documents. Despite their assistance, these machine-driven classifications often lack clarity as to why they were made. Present studies focusing on increasing classification transparency and clarity have emphasized improving taxonomies, but few have considered how modifying a dataset can foster greater understanding. To address this, our proposed approach involves a method for creating tailored, uniform subsets of a dataset that are specifically designed to provide clear interpretations of model predictions. We apply this innovation to a dataset of mathematical documents and compare its performance to that of traditional datasets, with the goal of discovering a method for preparing data that maximizes classification clarity. Our experimental results demonstrate that the newly formed subsets enable the model to make more predictable and consistent predictions, as confirmed by aggregate Interpolated Precision scores of 0.8059 for individual subsets and 0.8129 for combined subsets. Acceptance algorithm traditionally demands complete and ranked preference lists from each party. However, studies show that stable matchings can be achieved without requiring complete lists, and this paper confirms this conclusion by providing an instance in which using only a single-item preference list results in a stable matching. Moreover, we demonstrate that the proposed approach has an efficient runtime of O(n^2) and can be practically implemented using partially ranked preference lists generated by random samples. Our work even extends to more complex scenarios, such as multiple-sided markets with concave preferences. In these cases, we present a new algorithm that enables the construction of stable matchings using only single-item preference lists, and this solution has a runtime of O(n^3 log^2 n).

To address this limitation, we're exploring a novel approach that utilizes additional constraints to produce more accurate queries within the existing NMT framework. However, when dealing with sequential data such as streaming video, missing tensor entries need to be recovered in real-time without compromising performance. Existing streaming algorithms may not be effective when the data structure significantly changes over time, as seen in videos with rapid scene shifts or intense motion. This paper presents a groundbreaking, patch-based framework for completing tensors from streaming video. For each incoming frame, small image segments are identified by tracking them from the previous frame, and a unique tensor is created by combining similar segments from the new frame. This tensor is then restored using a real-time tensor completion algorithm. Our novel approach also introduces an enhanced patch tracking mechanism for efficient, dynamic tensor reconstruction and utilizes a Monte Carlo bisection method for fast, streaming-compatible rank estimation. Experimental results indicate the proposed methods surpass state-of-the-art tensor completion techniques in terms of performance and runtime efficiency.

(IGN) identifies natural dimensions in a network's hidden representations that can be modified to improve the model's ability to generalize. (IGN) consists of two modules: a graph attention module that trains a network to recognize connections between different input components, and a normalization module that adjusts the network's hidden representations to align with the graph structure. The investigation reveals how the periodic electric potential transforms Landau levels into oscillating bands, leading to specific oscillation patterns in response to magnetic field strength. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral expansion.

Our research involves presenting a probabilistic algorithm that takes an input high dimensional expander X with local spectral expansion at least 0.99, and generates a high dimensional expander Y located within X's covering space, sharing the same vertex set as X. These models do not incorporate gene flow and are therefore missing a critical component of eco-evolutionary change. We propose a stochastic diploid genetic model that includes migration and incorporates both neutral and adaptive drift, as well as demographic processes. Our findings show that a gene frequency in this model follows a specific geometric transformation when accounting for the resident and invader frequencies, resulting in a geometric morphing model. This model is scalable, independent of time and space coordinates, and reveals the inherent framework of stochastic evolutionary processes. Using invasive species and native species frequencies, we are able to derive invasive and native species frequencies that are similar to previous ecological models. Our results show that a stochastic diploid genetic model that incorporates migration not only simplifies the geometric morphing model but also reveals the invasive species tends to increase and converge towards fixation. We are also able to derive ecological models such as the resource-based invasion model by relaxing assumptions in our geometric morphing model. We are able to study co-evolutionary processes between two interacting species by assuming native and invasive species frequencies as variables in our geometric morphing model. Our results show that a stochastic diploid genetic model that incorporates migration not only simplifies the model but also reveals the complex invasion process. We are also able to study the outcomes of control strategies, such as sterilization programs, by analyzing the inverse of the inverse Jacobian of the geometric morphing model.

Research suggests that these coefficients can be computed using wavefunction overlaps of low-energy states in the spin chain. We have demonstrated that central charge, conformal dimensions, and operator product expansion coefficients are encoded in wavefunction overlaps, accompanied by universal corrections that rely on cyclic orbifold CFT content. annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and a broad range of related fields. However, the conventional approach to POS tagging is often hampered by the lack of tagged data. This problem can be alleviated to some extent by utilizing unlabeled texts. Nevertheless, the standard transfer learning technique fails to deliver optimal results due to the difficulty in accurately modeling the POS distribution. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a novel approach to learn the POS distribution using both lexical and contextual information from large corpora of raw texts. This method not only yields better performance but also requires minimal pre-processing of the data. Additionally, the POS distribution can be utilized in various applications such as information retrieval and natural language processing.

need for automated conversion of human-specified demands into precise, machine-readable specifications. taking the direct image of a partial order under a surjective epimorphism may not yield a partial order. In the category of sets, the best partial order approximation of the image in such a case is obtained by forming the cofibered image of the original preorder above the epimorphism. In categories satisfying regularity conditions, the existence of such a cofibered image of a partial order corresponds to the existence of the least upper bound among all partial orders within the category. This work explores conditions ensuring the existence of these cofibered images, which can be used in two distinct areas: the study of the consistency theory of second-order arithmetic, specifically for the foundation of inductive definition theory, and the analysis of a theory without choice, which involves predistributive lattices and involves generalizing a theorem of Baire for certain types of spaces.

the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationships between extreme rainfall events in the South Sudan region were analyzed over a 38-year period (1980-2018). The goal was to identify patterns and correlations of extreme events. The data exhibited two distinct types of dependence: local spatial dependence characterized extreme events within nearby areas, and a separate clustering of extreme events beyond immediate neighbors, which showed no local dependence. The analysis revealed significant correlations between the Log Normal distribution parameters of annual maximum rainfall in the Western and Central Rift Valley areas. The Western Rift Valley showed dependence with other rainfall locations both locally and in a broader sense, whereas the Central Rift Valley showed no local dependence but a separate clustering of extreme events. The presence of two distinct types of dependence precluded the use of a single multivariate spatial model for estimating the coefficients of spatial extent. Consequently, a separate model capturing the longer-range dependence for the Western Rift Valley was employed, while a model focusing solely on the Central Rift Valley's correlations with the Log Normal distribution parameters was used for the remaining locations, thus allowing the joint consideration of extreme rainfall locations in the South Sudan region.

Nevertheless, existing methods have not fully realized its potential due to a limitation in multimodal contrastive learning pipelines. To address this limitation, we introduce BOLD a comprehensive set of reforms that leverage multiple image-text pairs in line with unsupervised deep learning advancements. Comparative results demonstrate that our model outperforms the competitive baseline by a substantial margin.

Investigating the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films necessitates a deep comprehension of the effect of surface termination. Our studies achieved this through a combination of low-energy electron spectroscopy, X-ray absorption spectroscopy, and first-principles calculations to determine the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films and revealed that Cr-doped V$_2$O$_3$ films undergo a similar transition as undoped counterparts. However, further findings indicated that the surface terminations differ depending on the doping arrangement, with Cr-doped films exhibiting a distinct termination involving the substitution of V with Cr, in contrast to undoped films which involve the substitution of V without changing the oxygen layers. This terminations' impact on electronic properties were then explored through a comprehensive analysis of electronic structures, revealing a notable metal-insulator transition at the surface but not within bulk-like layers in the interior of V$_2$O$_3$. For Cr-doped films, the surface exhibits a distinct electron configuration involving 3d orbitals of V and Cr atoms at the surface, in addition to a sparingly filled t$_{2g}$ orbital. These observations resolve a long-standing debate over the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ and highlight the utility of spectroscopic techniques for understanding the relationship between chemical compositions and electronic properties.

Clebsch canonization has been proposed to convert Lie-Poisson equations into equivalent canonical Hamiltonian systems through a momentum map connection. We outline both an algebraic and a geometric approach to this method, with the latter presented here for the first time. Furthermore, we discovered an essential condition under which the momentum map leads to a complete symplectic structure on the resulting phase space from Lie-Poisson systems. Consequently, we applied the Clebsch transformation to the polar momenta of both the free rigid Rigid Rigid N-body problem and the 2-dimensional Euler equations on a vortex sheet, yielding the well-known Lagrange equations that govern these systems in canonical form.

Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are less sensitive to such transformations. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, our OCNs can leverage the benefits of existing deep learning frameworks while improving their robustness to orientation changes. Our proposed LGFs are constructed by selecting key Gabor filters and expressing them as sparse linear combinations of these markers, utilizing an $\ell_1$-norm regularization technique to derive a set of optimal filters via alternative iterations. Employing a sparsity-promoting optimization method allows us to selectively use a large collection of diverse Gabor filters with varying orientations in our feature representation. Our extensive experiments have demonstrated that OCNs, specifically OCNs with Local Average Pooling (OCN-LAP), outperform DCNNs and other baseline models in terms of sensitivity to orientation changes. Moreover, our method automatically selects a limited number of critical Gabor filters, resulting in reduced memory requirements and computational costs.

a measure of association in statistical analysis. The strength of evidence for linear correlation is often evaluated using a hypothesis test, resulting in a p-value. Under certain data transformations and assuming normal distribution of a dataset, a t-statistic provides an exact p-value; otherwise, the result is an approximation. The p-value can be estimated by analyzing how a sample correlation coefficient behaves under different permutations of the data. Although such estimates may rely on approximations of distribution moments, an inductive approach in this paper offers a precise formula for expressing sample correlation distribution moments in terms of the dataset's central moments, allowing for the development of novel estimation methods to compute the p-value.

an increase in research on explainable recommendation systems. Among these, post-hoc methods have been identified as the most practical solutions for addressing the transparency issue. Two leading post-hoc techniques, XRank and GRU, have been widely applied, but they have limitations in occlusion matrix precision. This issue can be resolved by combining the two techniques, as proposed in the novel approach, e-Rank. e-Rank enhances occlusion matrix prediction by leveraging XRank's item diversity and GRU's user memory, and was tested on real-world datasets. Experimental results demonstrated the method's effectiveness in improving occlusion matrix accuracy, and its practical application in ranking tasks. As graphene's electrical resistance is highly sensitive to temperature and the presence of magnetic fields, it can serve as an efficient component in a new generation of thermomechanical devices. Furthermore, it has a non-linear electrical response when subjected to a specific magnetic field, which enables the creation of compact magnetic devices. We demonstrate a tiny graphene-based device that exhibits distinct phenomena: its electrical current changes in proportion to the square of the applied magnetic field when subjected to a specific DC voltage and a sweeping magnetic field. This device, which is no thicker than 1 nm, has successfully merged the boundaries between millimeter-scale thermomechanical devices and nanoscale quantum devices, enabling the development of smaller, more complex and interconnected quantum systems.

Nonetheless, it remains uncertain whether these assumptions can be effectively determined from the data itself, rather than relying on pre-existing knowledge. In this study, we present a novel functional learning framework in which we aim to detect whether the underlying distribution of outcomes follows a specific, known form. By exploring this problem in relation to kernel ridge regression, a non-parametric approach that relies on a pre-specified kernel, we demonstrate its applications for both computational and statistical benefits. In order to address the resulting statistical complexities, we develop a simplified maximum likelihood approach, which yields a computationally efficient algorithm and statistically analyzes its properties under the assumption of a known covariance function. A cross-validation procedure is then proposed to non-parametrically test the validity of this assumption, leading to an algorithm that effectively detects whether the data follows the assumed Gaussian distribution. Moreover, we examine the scenario in which the covariance function is unknown, discovering that the maximum likelihood approach continues to be effective with the incorporation of a specific regularization technique. A computational analysis of the statistical properties of our methods reveals robust empirical results, even when the data does not conform to the assumed distribution. Ultimately, we reflect on the implications of these findings in the context of the broader functional learning paradigm, highlighting both the limitations and ramifications of assuming knowledge of crucial statistical components.

To investigate how X-rays affect organic molecules, we examine young stellar objects (YSOs) with massive outflows containing polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), using the Chandra X-ray telescope. We discover that dust clouds surrounding these YSOs may not entirely block X-rays, allowing them to penetrate to just centimeters from the star. In YSOs with massive outflows, X-rays may have sufficient energy to alter the composition of water and organic molecules, possibly leading to their simplification. We find no direct correlation between X-ray intensity and the presence of PAHs or water-rich molecules, indicating that dust clouds significantly shield the surrounding environment. Furthermore, highly ionized gases, indicative of extremely intense X-ray emission, are absent in YSOs with massive outflows containing PAHs. We suggest that massive outflows may have a secondary role in altering the composition of water and organic molecules, rather than the primary source. Instead, X-rays may primarily drive this change. We explore potential local mechanisms for regulating X-ray intensity, such as magnetic fields, and suggest observing neutral gases near hot stars to understand how X-rays affect water and organic molecules, including PAHs, at YSOs.

In this study, we explore ways to enhance the visibility of sclerai landmarks in ultrasound images by utilizing a learning-based approach that combines different modalities. Our approach includes pre-processing techniques such as non-uniformity correction, followed by a novel deep learning framework that pairs a convolutional neural network with an active shape model to pin down distinctive landmark features. Our research indicates that this method achieves precise and reproducible results comparable to those obtained through manual ultrasonic assessment. Furthermore, we propose a novel deep learning-based approach for generating comprehensive maps of spinal curvature by using pairs of sclerai landmark images as reference points. Our findings suggest that this approach can provide accurate and reliable curvature information along the entire spine with high resolution and precise control, and that it may potentially replace the need for manual ultrasonic assessment in scoliosis assessment.

Therefore, the dynamic nature of these experiences is not typically viewed as an essential component of the risk factor domain. However, the emerging concept of biological embedding suggests that both early life exposures and the present circumstances can shape an individual's health responses, and these exposures can change over time. This article offers a framework for analyzing early life experiences and employs examples of two significant chronic diseases, hypertension and obesity, to demonstrate the significance of considering these dynamic processes. In contrast to typical cooling effects, 'hothouse' climates are distinguished by a blocked window region for water vapor, which has led to theories of resulting temperature inversions and altered cloud formations. Prior climate modeling has failed to resolve turbulent air motions and cloud dynamics directly, leaving significant gaps in understanding hothouse climate processes. In this research, simulations resolving convection explicitly found that 'hothouse' low atmospheric heating shifts the water cycle from steady state to a periodic regime, characterized by intense precipitation and long dry spells. The transition to this regime was associated with increased local precipitation and cloud cover, along with a positive climate feedback that may stabilize 'hothouse' environments. The research implies the presence of a new type of temporal atmospheric self-organization, affecting both cloud formations and erosion in hothouse climates.

This study aims to establish a new approach for identifying the 3-D geometric characteristics of significant, swirling motions within wall turbulence, allowing these structures to be directly integrated into existing models and thereby improving their predictive capabilities. This approach is applied here to reconstruct a 3-D picture of wall turbulence for various wall-bound flow scenarios across a wide range of friction Reynolds numbers, with a particular focus on understanding the impact of these structures on skin-friction drag and the transfer of momentum between inner and outer flow regions. Analysis of this approach reveals the geometric self-similarity of these structures across various wall-bound flow scenarios and suggests that the hairpin vortex packet may be a common underlying flow mechanism. This understanding is then used to propose a 2nd-streamwise-estuarine-coherent structure model for laminar flow conditions, leading to the prediction that flow structures at low Reynolds numbers may not significantly influence skin-friction drag, whereas high Reynolds numbers may experience greater drag reductions due to these structures. However, the present approach suggests that the efficacy of these structures could be reduced at high Reynolds numbers due to increased flow disorganization. This suggests the possibility of achieving optimal drag reduction by selectively activating or suppressing vortex packets based on their geometric characteristics in accordance with the local Reynolds number and the inherent flow structures present.

The effective implementation of the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield framework yields an energy lower bound, with corresponding self-dual equations whose solutions manifest as the limiting solitons that achieve this bound. The lower bound on energy, known as the Bogomol'nyi bound, exhibits proportionality to a topological charge denoted by Q and defined through a spatial integral of the spatial component of the gauge field. This study details soliton profiles for self-dual solitons in two-dimensional space-time and presents an analytic solution for a specific model that incorporates a 't Hooft ansatz for the gauge field, resulting in a modified Skyrme model that excludes the gauge field and is known to admit compact, topologically non-trivial solitons. However, this study finds that the Born-Infeld term prevents the solitons from being completely non-trivial within the model.

The research assesses the efficiency of SMOTE, its modified versions (Borderline and ADASYN), and random oversampling methods using 22 datasets from diverse domains, considering different machine learning algorithms and feature extraction techniques. for augmenting existing data to enhance the learning capacity of reinforcement and imitation learning from experienced models. The policy cloning approach, a fundamental component of various learning techniques, is our focus, as it leverages the expertise of a guiding model to shape a student model's behavior. To accelerate the policy cloning process, we introduce a data augmentation method that generates an extensive variety of successful student actions without significantly increasing the required computations. Our approach, which can be seamlessly integrated into both supervised and imitation learning frameworks, is versatile and adaptable to different policy cloning algorithms. Key to our augmentation technique is Deep Reach-Average-Zero (Drzo), an innovative reward function that analyzes the environment's response to zero-reward actions, uncovering understudied opportunities for exploration. We discovered (i) unique zero-reward states, (ii) spur-of-the-moment actions, and (iii) essential skill combinations that were overlooked by traditional methods. Our experimental results show that our data augmentation technique significantly improves the efficiency of various policy cloning algorithms across multiple benchmark scenarios, leading to shorter training times and more effective performance.

iggs bosons ($hh$) paired with a vector boson ($W$ or $Z$) using a massive dataset of 139 inverse femtobarns of proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy has been carried out utilizing the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The research explores final states in which the vector boson decays into electrons and neutrinos or into electrons and other electrons and neutrinos, and each Higgs boson decays into pairs of $b$-quarks. It aims to detect the $Vhh$ signals from non-resonant and resonant production of $hh$, with the latter predicted in certain Standard Model extensions. For the former, a 95% confidence upper limit of 183 times the predicted Standard Model cross-section has been observed, whereas for the latter an expected limit of 87 times is anticipated assuming the expected Standard Model kinematics. Furthermore, limits are imposed on the coupling modifiers of the Higgs bosons, as well as cross-section limits derived for the resonant production of $H$, $A$, or both, in the mass ranges specified. Finally, constraints have been placed in the parameter space of two-Higgs-doublet models.

An appropriate assessment methodology involves collecting diverse driving data, such as manual controls, vehicle velocity, and surrounding traffic information, in different contexts. Recent advancements in connected and vehicle information technology have significantly enhanced the availability of this data. This study provides an overview of the major commercial driving behavior evaluation methodologies utilized in the automotive industry today. These methodologies differ in their approaches to assessment design, data collection, driving scenarios, and evaluation indicators. A few prominent companies, including Daimler and BMW, are leading the development of benchmarking programs that offer transparent assessment methods and regular updates. The industry consensus is that a single, fixed protocol is insufficient for a comprehensive assessment of commercial driving behavior. Instead, the collective outcome of various approaches is considered a more accurate representation of the state-of-the-art. The surveyed companies are involved in industry partnerships, such as the PReVENT program, which aim to standardize data protocols and foster a shared understanding of driving behavior. The industry is also engaged in the use of surrogate safety indicators, such as time to collision and driver attention metrics, which are being employed by leading companies including Volkswagen and General Motors. The survey of commercial driving behavior evaluation methodologies exposes the necessity for a standardized data protocol, encapsulating the entire spectrum of driving situations, and is therefore seeking potential contributions from the research community to develop a more comprehensive assessment of commercial driving behavior.

2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text when provided with a scene image and a segmented task involving individual word recognition.
The primary contribution of this research is the largest and most comprehensive OOV dataset to date, incorporating various image modalities (handwritten, printed, and scene texts) with words not seen during model training.
The evaluation involved leading cutting-edge OCR models and demonstrated the effectiveness of semantic segmentation in aiding holistic word recognition on OOV challenges.

While it's well-documented that this algorithm converges when a solution exists, a linear convergence rate is achieved only if both the solution and the reference coupling have the same support. Considering that structured stochastic processes might help resolve ambiguities in the problem, a new variant of the Sinkhorn algorithm is introduced that incorporates geometric flow. Geometric flow is a natural representation of transport processes that can be used to improve the convergence of the algorithm. 

A key finding of the study is that the algorithm with geometric flow converges at a rate of $O(k^{-2})$, with $k$ denoting the number of iterations, regardless of whether the reference coupling is generic or has a specific structure. Importantly, similar fast convergence is inherited by various iterative geometric flows. To illustrate the advantage of the algorithm with geometric flow, comparative analyses are performed on a reference coupling that has a simple form with known properties, revealing accelerated convergence for certain structured couplings. 

Overall, a novel geometric flow-based algorithm offers a flexible, efficient, and potentially structured solution to the Schrödinger problem, offering advantages over traditional unstructured solutions like the gradient descent algorithm for orthogonal projections. As such, it may be beneficial for applications like data distribution mapping in parallel computing systems.

a less than optimal strategy known as probability-matching, which means choosing options based on their reward probabilities, as opposed to the optimal strategy, maximization, which involves consistently selecting the option with the highest reward.  Despite years of study, the factors leading to probability-matching are still unclear and a theoretical explanation for this phenomenon is still lacking.  We developed a model, called a 'weight-ceremony' theory, which helps explain why and when probability-matching occurs.  According to our model, animals with limited capacity for short-term memory tend to give greater importance to recent events when recalling past experiences, which leads to a situation where its prediction and recall systems are out of alignment, resulting in probability-matching.  We tested our model through simulations and found that a specific form of learning, called 'constant learning rate' learning, which has limited memory capabilities and a unique combination of updated valuations, results in probability-matching, whereas all other forms of learning with limited memory, as well as maximization, do not result in probability-matching.  Furthermore, we have found a way to directly test our model's predictions in an experiment involving monkeys.  Our study indicates that a simple, memory-based explanation can provide a theoretical foundation for understanding probability-matching.

A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between scalability and validity: methods that handle a large number of qubits tend to produce negative probabilities, whereas those that guarantee a correct probability distribution cannot be scaled. To address these concerns, we propose and implement a new scheme that combines both principles. Specifically, we adapt and implement a standard iterative Bayesian calibration method within a newly established probability space to mitigate measurement errors. This approach is validated through experiments on both a superconducting qubit system and a ion trap system. The improved efficiency and generality of this approach make it a compelling approach for calibrating noisy quantum gates.

Current research on assistive teleoperation and shared control focuses on developing methods for the robot to determine the desired task based on human joystick inputs. Typically, this is done by using an internal map that links joystick inputs to specific tasks: for instance, pressing the joystick to the left indicates the desire to move a plate, while pressing it to the right signifies a cup. Lastly, a relatively small exchange field was applied to the underlying superconducting host, indicating that the surface exchange enhancement has a significant effect and cannot be overlooked in the analysis. a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, both of which can be learned through unsupervised methods. Experimental findings show that the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis results in improved steganographic performance with regard to capacity-distortion metrics.

To characterize the parton motions, we apply principles from solid-state physics, describing them as independent particles moving according to specific, collective patterns. However, test code can be compromised by suboptimal design or implementation choices referred to as test smells. These shortcomings can significantly undermine the quality of software systems by exacerbating difficulties in comprehension, amplifying maintenance complexities, and making systems more susceptible to bugs and errors. Prior studies have investigated the likely consequences of test smells on test code. Despite their focus, a knowledge gap remains regarding the perspectives of developers regarding these issues. To fill this knowledge gap, a study empirically examined how software developers perceive the level of impact test smells have on test code. The investigation analyzed the perspectives of developers from six open-source projects, inquiring about the influence of test smells on test code and seeking descriptions of instances where test smell consequences had been encountered. The results show that while many developers consider test smells to have little to no impact on test code, instances of significant consequences can occur. The implications of this discovery for developers seeking to prioritize smell refactoring are discussed.

challenge exists in assessing the influence of interventions or causes on continuous outcome variables. For interventions focused on a single unit (e.g., a patient or a firm), researchers often measure outcomes before and after the intervention, leveraging difference-in-differences (DiD) analysis to control for confounding variables using observational pre-intervention data. However, the widely applied DiD method often rests on assumptions that are challenging to substantiate, particularly when dealing with small sample sizes. In this context, Bayesian approaches hold promise in mitigating these concerns. A significant limitation of existing Bayesian DiD methods lies in their failure to account for the impact of interventions on continuous outcome variables, a gap this paper aims to address by proposing a Bayesian framework for estimating the impact of single-unit interventions on continuous outcome variables. A numerical evaluation and an empirical case study demonstrate the efficacy of this approach.

The paper derives formulas for the distribution of persistent cycles via mathematical computations and exhibits both theoretical and practical instances where these cycles' characteristics are applicable. It can model materials' microstructures as persistent cycles, offering an alternative to the commonly used small world model. The study demonstrates that persistent cycles exhibit scale invariance, with examples showing their utility in experimentally obtained data and a simulated dataset based on the COSMOS particle irradiation database. The research reveals that persistent cycles' characteristics are applicable to random geometric graphs' exifacial, 2-coloring patterns. The study also discusses connections to random complex theories such as the Erdos-Renyi complex and the (1+t) fractional Delaunay complex.

We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using estimated depth and segmentation maps to calculate the camera's position through iterative closest point alignment. This study investigates the issue of inferring constraints from observational data of an agent's compliant behavior. Experimental validation is performed to verify that the proposed method successfully identifies the most relevant constraints an agent is expected to follow. Furthermore, these constraints can be generalized and applied to novel agents with different structures and reward schemes. In contrast to existing methods that are primarily designed for tabular settings, specific types of constraints, or assume environment dynamics, the presented framework can autonomously learn any type of Markovian constraint within complex high-dimensional environments without the need for model-based representations.

Most network measures were initially developed for simple undirected networks.
As a result, weighted network extensions were created to incorporate weight-based information, particularly for calculating the local clustering coefficient.
We discovered that not all these extensions can guarantee the preservation of their underlying mathematical definitions.
Our analysis covered various weighted network representations within the scope of both directed and undirected networks.
For many commonly used edge weights, like length or cost, undirected networks may appear more consistent than directed ones, even though the underlying structure is directional.
Consequently, our study suggests that weighted network research should adhere to the following principles: (a) its connections must be represented as directed edges to preserve the directional structure, and (b) the resulting computations should align with their weighted extensions.
We verified the validity of several widely used clustering extensions for both theoretical and practical applications.
One of the extensions we validated is the weighted local clustering coefficient developed by Newman.
Our research indicates that only weighted triangles' total weight or the number of them should be considered for this measure, and never the average radius or circumference of these objects.
We also discovered that using edge weights derived from distances can lead to issues if they become zero during the analysis.
Our findings suggest that further research on weighted networks should focus on developing more realistic and necessary mathematical representations for various applications.

systems into machine learning models is physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). These models have been observed to perform well with smaller training datasets, excel in generalizing outcomes, and reduce training time. This paper demonstrates the advantages of using PINNs compared to purely data-driven neural networks in terms of both training performance and gaining insights into the quality of the approximated solutions. By considering PINNs that are trained with an underlying ordinary differential equation, we derive a strict upper limit on their prediction error, applicable even for data not included in the training phase and without prior knowledge of the true solution. As a crucial step in verifying PINNs, this error estimation provides an assurance of their reliability. To exemplify the practical application of our results, we test the error estimator on two theoretical test problems, including one that showcases the capabilities of PINNs in handling partial differential equations with space-time dependencies.

air pollution modeling is crucial. Leveraging advances in big data analytics and machine learning has led to breakthroughs in air pollution modeling frameworks. This discussion highlights recent breakthroughs and proposes enhancements from the viewpoints of geostatistics and machine learning. Future developments will integrate learning algorithms with spatial analysis, allowing for the incorporation of spatial correlations in the prediction process. This integration is expected to improve the precision of existing air pollution models, thereby enhancing the efficacy of exposure assessments in epidemiologic studies.

lower bound for the eigenvalues of a design matrix, generated by linear bandit algorithms that incur sub-linear regret in action spaces with constant curvature properties. In specific cases where the action space has a constant Hessian, we can precisely determine all eigenvalue options for the design matrix. By leveraging these findings, we derive sharper bounds on the performance of linear bandit algorithms and demonstrate their applicability to well-known action spaces such as the real line, closed intervals, and spheres. Our theoretical analysis yields general algorithms capable of outperforming state-of-the-art linear bandit methods, particularly in scenarios where the design matrix exhibits ill-conditioned properties. For instance, we showcase the effectiveness of our approach in context-free scenarios where arm identities are not explicitly provided, and the arms' identity is coupled with the observation noise level. Furthermore, we show that our algorithm can be adapted for context-dependent settings, and compare its performance to established methods within this environment.

the valley Hall effect, where different types of electron flows, determined by specific indices, are observed.  Our research, however, demonstrates that this effect can be more accurately described by the orbital Hall effect, where the indices representing "valleys" are replaced with a distinct physical measurement called Landau level index.  Furthermore, we find that the valley Hall conductivity can be completely translated into the Landau level Hall conductivity, with the latter being significantly more predictable due to its dependence on a quantifiable variable, the Landau level index, rather than the elusive "valley" index.  Our translation also reveals that the valley Hall conductivity is essentially a measure of the change in electron population between the two valleys that change with magnetic field strength, whereas the orbital Hall conductivity directly represents the overall population change in all particles in a valley as the magnetic field changes.

Over the past two years, research has gained momentum in graph adversarial attacks but Graph Classification remains an understudied area. The indirect utilization of Reinforcement Learning methods for graph classification, given that datasets involve discrete graphs with labels, stands in contrast to traditional approaches that use direct gradient optimization. A novel approach described here utilizes photometric data from multiple catalogs by incorporating the magnitudes in a novel source matching algorithm. This technique involves calculating the log-likelihood of a match by taking the exponential of the sum of the logarithmic probabilities. The magnitude-based log-likelihood is determined through a comparison of the input and reference catalogs. This newly proposed algorithm is compared to a previous method that relied solely on position-based log-likelihoods and was tested using various WISE-based catalogs. The results show that incorporating magnitude information leads to an improvement in accuracy and a reduction in up to 50% of incorrect associations when matches have low log-likelihood values. Furthermore, the combined log-likelihoods of position and magnitude perform similarly to the magnitude-based log-likelihoods, but with the added benefit of handling matches where the input and reference catalogs have differing numbers of measurements. The code is publicly available for download.

It has been proven previously that a hypergraph fulfilling the conditions of minimum size 'l' possesses the property C(2l+1, l+1). formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise hundreds of thousands of interconnected concepts. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and exploration. However, existing visualisation tools predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation system designed to seamlessly balance the exploration of all concept relationships and large hierarchical structures. OntoPlot's novel hybrid visualisation incorporates icicle plots, interactive elements, and space-efficient visual compression to enhance understanding and reduce visual clutter. Through a user study involving domain experts, we compared OntoPlot's usability to that of Protégé, the primary ontology editing tool, finding that OntoPlot surpassed expectations in facilitating association-related tasks and earned widespread endorsement from domain specialists.

inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to facilitate semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Inter-domain loss aims to derive a common speech-text representation through a shared neural network, whereas CycleGAN leverages cycle consistency and identity mapping to preserve input characteristics after cross-domain conversion. As our experiments cannot directly evaluate the cross-domain speech-text connection due to complete dataset privacy, we employ meta-learning to simulate privileged information and render the inter-domain loss applicable. We evaluate our approach on the AFEW+ database, a privacy-protected emotion recognition dataset. The experimental outcomes show our method surpasses the baseline in accuracy, with significant improvements of 8.4% and 12.1% when using 5% and 10% of training data relative to a fully supervised baseline.

how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is restricted to simplified simulations due to limitations in dealing with complex environments. This paper establishes a novel approach to addressing this limitation by incorporating deep learning techniques and removing the need for explicit state representations in mental frameworks. Utilizing a deep learning method to incorporate prior knowledge, we create a mental framework consisting of self-similar neural networks that learn to represent causally interconnected factors contributing to uncertainty. Distinguishing our approach from conventional methods, we showcase its efficacy with large-scale simulations and highlight its potential to expand to more complex real-world scenarios.

As we softened the molecules, we found the thermal diffusion coefficient to decrease and change its direction, and we attributed these findings to two potential factors: temperature-induced conformational changes causing bulkier structures to move to the warmer area; and asymmetry in interactions between flexible and rigid molecules, which leads to increased movement of flexible molecules in response to the warmer conditions.

Effective evaluation by an NLP model depends on its ability to identify patterns in written content, even in cases where the writing quality is subpar. Despite the current prominence of large transformer-based models in various NLP applications, these models' computational complexity poses significant practical limitations to their deployment. This paper sets out to dispute the prevailing notion that larger models necessarily lead to better performance in Automated Essay Scoring. To this end, we provide an in-depth examination of how multiple factors affect the outcomes of smaller models, which we then demonstrate by achieving competitive results in the 2019 Kaggle Grader state-of-the-l literature competition using our proposed approaches.

nostic domain shift in domain adaptive pedestrian detection is the prevalence of false positives. As labeling each target domain's boxes is impractical, researchers focus on suppressing false positives in target domains using unsupervised methods. Current approaches often rely on modifying the box prediction distribution to avoid over-confidence in incorrect boxes. However, existing confidence modulation techniques mainly rely on a single global confidence scale across entire images. This global scale is insufficient in domains with large objects close to the camera, as object scale greatly affects one's confidence in accuracy. This paper proposes a novel scale-aware confidence modulation module that locally adapts to the object scale to avoid over-confidence in incorrect boxes. This module has been successfully integrated into the popular Siamese objective neural network, producing outstanding results on the challenging benchmark ADAS++ dataset.

A novel deep learning technique combines two processes: one transforms audio in a specific representation while removing unwanted components, and another converts the modified audio into a high-quality music recording. We experimented with various approaches for the auxiliary task of eliminating microphone distortion, a more pressing problem than typically encountered noise and echo effects. Our research indicates that a straightforward maximum likelihood training strategy yields the best results when dealing with common microphone distortion patterns. Furthermore, our method demonstrates its adaptability in addressing a broader range of echo lengths by incorporating a convolutional layer. Lastly, our evaluation reveals a substantial improvement in music quality over current benchmark techniques.

Our perceptual study revealed that individuals tend to more readily notice errors in underarm throws where the point of release occurs early, in contrast to late releases. Conversely, in the case of overarm throws, both early and late points of release are more challenging to identify. Furthermore, we discovered that when an observer witnesses an underarm throw with an incorrect point of release, it is easier to identify the deviation if the ball is released beyond the throwing person's shoulder rather than before it. Our results also encompass the examination of various other release styles (underarm versus overarm) and the associated proportions of expert (fielders) and novice (non-fielders) who successfully identified the deviation.

The proposed Seq2DRNN architecture synergizes a sequential encoder with tree-structured decoding enhanced by a syntax-aware attention mechanism, differing from prior syntax-based NMT methods that rely on dependency parsing models. We developed the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP) to create a comprehensive database containing the full range of binding energies between molecules and an amorphous water surface model. This involved applying classical force fields to bind small intermolecular compounds on water surfaces. Our research included water surface binding energies for 62 distinct compounds involving 41 molecules, encompassing carbohydrates, amino acids, organic acids, nitrogen-containing compounds, metals, and other substances. We computed binding energy values in ranges from 20 meV for small molecules up to 300 meV for larger compounds arranged in multi-molecular arrangements. Each binding energy had an associated error margin of around 70 meV. This database can serve as a resource for developing complex astrochemical models, and our method offers a template for investigating more intricate surface environments.

about a mysterious quantum state using an efficiently manageable number of copies. Our key contributions are two innovations. Firstly, we devise a technique to determine the most probable measurement outcome from a set of k state replicas with a reduced number of measurements. Our analysis shows that the required number of measurements is directly proportional to the number of k state replicas. Our proposed method achieves the optimal measurement outcome determination with the fewest possible measurements as defined by the Dvoretzky-R James theorem. Secondly, we extend our initial approach to identify the shortest list of probabilities that can accurately represent the unknown distribution with high confidence, even when dealing with an infinite number of probabilities. Our solutions to both problems are highly versatile, applicable to various models of quantum states, and offer substantial computational advantages. Our study focuses on the homogeneous model, presenting both theoretical and practical results, which include an efficient, classical, and real-world compatible poly(n) time algorithm for optimizing the shortest list of probabilities. Our findings demonstrate that the optimal list has a logarithmic size relative to n, the number of probabilities. Our algorithms are based on the concept of majorization, a core principle in probability theory. Our work showcases the usefulness of the k-tensor power of a matrix, providing a linear operator that can help determine the most probable measurement outcome. Our study explores the limitations of our approach, presenting a lower bound on the number of measurements required to accurately identify certain symmetric multivariate distributions.

In order to address this issue, we propose a concept called sibylvariance, which refers to the use of data transformations that can vary class labels and lead to greater diversity of input data. To this end, we compile a collection of sibylvariance data transformations from text and apply them to eight NLP tasks in order to create a diverse dataset. Utilizing our sibylvariance data transformations, we are able to enhance the performance of models on eight different NLP tasks, including parsing, semantics, and language understanding, by improving their ability to generalize. Importantly, we find that the benefits of sibylvariance are most pronounced on smaller datasets, indicating that it can effectively mitigate the issues of limited data and potential data biases. Moreover, our sibylvariance data transformations are available for use in research, allowing researchers to easily incorporate them into their existing projects.

on previous experience to rapidly acquire new skills or adapt to new environments by utilizing previous training data more efficiently. In order to achieve this, the task of selecting the most relevant previous tasks for learning can be simplified. We propose the 'Maximum a Posteriori' (MAP) approach, a unified framework for making task selection decisions based on maximizing the posterior probability of success. We show that this MAP approach encompasses traditional metrics such as transfer metrics, and that its connection to risk-based evaluation metrics like cross-validation can be theoretically proven. We empirically confirm the success of the MAP approach with its neighbors, a neighborhood-based approach that leverages similarity to identify relevant tasks, and demonstrate especially improved performance in the case of the latter method.

-art machine translation models can aid in adapting to low-resource languages despite limited data, albeit resulting in oversized models that are impractical for deployment. To combat this, Knowledge Distillation is an often-used method to create high-performance yet lightweight models. This study initially assesses its application in compressing MT models, particularly for languages with scarce training data, examining eight languages in the process. Notably, it's discovered that distillation-based model performance variability heavily relies on several preconditions, making it a somewhat unreliable compression approach. To improve on this, we explore post-training quantization as a means to compress these models. Ultimately, while distillation was found effective in certain low-resource languages, it's shown that quantization produces more consistent performance outcomes across a broader range of languages, particularly those with the least available training data in MT.

graph F, denoted by ex(n, F), is defined as the maximum number of edges in an F-free r-uniform graph on n vertices. The Turan density of F, denoted by pi(F), is defined as the limit of the maximum number of edges over the total possible number of edges as the number of vertices approaches infinity. Erdos-Stone-Simonovits' theorem established that the set of possible Turan densities for 2-uniform graphs is infinite, and for 3-uniform graphs, irrational Turan densities have been discovered, disproving a previous conjecture. We investigate whether irrational Turan densities exist in certain cases and show lower bounds on pi(F) for specific types of 3-uniform F-free graphs. We also formulate a conjecture that irrational Turan densities exist for 3-uniform F-free graphs where no two vertices share more than one edge.

identifying abnormalities on chest X-rays is limited by the laborious task of gathering and annotating training data. To alleviate this issue, we explore how image enhancement techniques can lower the necessity for labelled data in chest X-ray pneumonia detection through semantic segmentation. By training fully convolutional neural network models on subsets of various sizes from a total dataset, each model undergoes a different image enhancement while its performance is compared to a baseline model trained without such augmentations on the entire dataset. Ultimately, we discovered that using rotate and mixup image enhancement methods leads to a significant reduction of 70% in labelled data requirements while demonstrating comparable results to the baseline in AUC and mean IoU in our experiments.

This paper proposes a unified image captioning framework that excels across various domains and can effortlessly adapt to multiple captioning styles. We incorporate a flexible prompt learning system that enables the model to absorb data from multiple domains, ensuring its performance remains strong in each domain. Additionally, we optimize the prompts using dynamic vectors within a word embedding space, reducing the reliance on manual tuning and significantly enhancing the model's capabilities. At the inference stage, our model allows for the generation of custom caption styles by simply selecting the most suitable prompt, yielding outstanding results in COCO Karpathy and TextCaps benchmarks.

Previous attempts to define harm in philosophical literature have failed to address various real-world examples, leading some to consider abandoning the concept of harm. The existing definitions of harm, largely reliant on causality, surprisingly overlook the use of causal models and actual causality theories. This paper presents a new definition of qualitative harm, grounded in causal models, and demonstrates its application to both general and artificial scenarios. The proposed definition focuses on whether a treatment rendered an outcome more unlikely, which aligns with existing notions of harm seen in legal and regulatory contexts.

The integration with OpenCV and the development of automated PySpark wrapper generation tool expands the capabilities of Spark's ecosystem. The MMLSpark library is accompanied by an extensive collection of tools and features. By contrast, single-system implementations tend to be intricate and expensive to build. To tackle this challenge, we rely on adversarial training to create a unified model that learns direct translation. Our approach involves employing adversarial discriminative models to guide the speech-to-text model to disregard intermediate representations during processing. In this paper, we address this issue by introducing an innovative deep learning-based method that combines data from various sources to enable more accurate predictions of thermal energy consumption. The proposed approach involves the development of two interconnected models. A initial model calculates the temperature based on the power consumption, while a subsequent enhanced temperature predictor fine-tunes this output to provide more accurate temperature estimates and ultimately enable more precise energy consumption predictions. The proposed technique has been tested on three distinct datasets, significantly outperforming existing baseline methods by an average of 15 to 26% in terms of accuracy. The proposed technique can also provide user-specific forecasts, thereby enabling more personalized suggestions for reducing energy consumption.

resolved the issues affecting AI performance, notably changing conditions and "out-of-the-box" reasoning. Nature-inspired algorithms such as the Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) algorithm, which mimics the process by which ants discover paths in nature, offer promising solutions. In this research, a novel ACO approach called "multiplexing" was developed to tackle complex optimization problems. The proposed method leverages the idea that ant multiplexing can lead to the creation of robust chemical signals, thus overcoming previous limitations. A comparative analysis was conducted to evaluate the performance of this novel multiplexor-based ACO (MACO) approach against existing methods, including non-interactive ACO (NACO) and a hybrid local-global search technique. The results show that MACO successfully achieves better solution quality and reduced computational costs compared to NACO, thereby confirming its viability as a reliable optimization tool. Additionally, a comparative evaluation of MACO, Non-Convex Convex Relaxation (CCR), and a hybrid local-global search approach revealed that MACO performs competitively with respect to both solution quality and computational effort. Furthermore, an in-depth analysis of MACO's properties highlighted its potential to achieve robust, wide-range solution quality, thus addressing a critical gap in the field. Finally, the proposed approach demonstrates the ability to handle increasingly complex CSTR design problems with multiple constraints effectively.

detection on chest CT scans poses significant difficulties despite considerable advancements. The issue often arises due to annotation biases affecting traditional supervised segmentation techniques, which rely on detailed boundary markings. To resolve these issues and minimize labeling expenses, we introduce an innovative framework that utilizes image-level labels, thereby facilitating unbiased supervision. Our approach leverages a deep, generative CT synthesis network to convert two-dimensional images into three-dimensional block datasets. By employing block-level supervison with 3D transverse reconstruction and context-based loss functions, we effectively train our model. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in producing accurate volumes for COVID-19 detection, both in individual cases and overall community assessment.

crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise method that leverages in-depth anatomical knowledge of the spine to aid in accurate vertebrae localization and identification. By employing a novel key point localization model, vertebrae center activation maps are generated, which are subsequently adjusted along the spine's central axis to produce optimized activation points. To ensure uniform spacing between these points, an optimal spacing method is employed. As our method is influenced by the development of spine-related diseases, we incorporate a hereditary model to empirically determine the optimal number of activation points for each specific medical instance. To facilitate training, a large synthetic dataset of normal and pathological spines has been created. Experimental results demonstrate that our method produces the most accurate results compared to previous techniques both in terms of localization and identification.

Within an extremely high level of electron interaction with the surrounding electromagnetic field, temporary variations in the field energy lead to a steady state formation of an entwined state confined at the center of the barrier. As an incoming electron's energy aligns with that of this confined state, it undergoes rapid, inelastic collision resulting in emission of a cavity-generated photon. This phenomenon is being researched as a potential method to produce unconventional light.

spring-based actuators can boost energy efficiency and performance but complicate the controller's design. We diverge from the conventional approach of optimizing controllers for specific actuators and instead develop a general controller capable of working with various spring-based actuators. We start by modeling a general spring-based actuator and then apply a model-predictive controller to a three-dimensional quadruped model. We highlight the controller's flexibility by demonstrating its effectiveness with both artificial and real spring-based actuators. We also compare our approach to traditional methods, especially since the results show comparable walking outcomes while using up to 90% less power. The resulting controller's open-source code is available for further research.

Our algorithm's performance is initially tested with GHZ states composed of up to seven qubits via simulations that utilize state vectors and random measurements. We also use numerical methods to determine the closest separable states for maximally entangled multipartite X-states. Our results indicate that NISQ devices may leverage the VSV's efficiency to tackle the challenging full separability problem due to their limited quantum capacity. Prior research in a slab geometry setting showed that the drive mechanism requires collisions, but our simulations show that in the absence of collisions, there is still a small-scale, electron temperature-driven instability that shares similarities with the microtearing mode. Despite this, our simulations show that the amplitude of this instability is much lower than what's seen in collisional settings. Notably, our study also shows that the species conservation law that's often applied in plasma physics is not relevant in this context.

led researchers to investigate fashion instance-level image retrieval, which involves finding matching images. Building upon this, the concept of fashion attribute manipulation, which modifies a specific attribute while retaining others, has emerged. This enables users to search not only identical items but also similar items with specific attributes. However, this task is challenging due to the difficulty in defining attributes and preserving query uniqueness. Although fashion instance-level image retrieval and fashion attribute manipulation pose significant challenges, they are underexposed as separate tasks. In response, we propose a novel approach called fashion attribute evolution, which incorporates both concepts. This task involves developing a method to generate new images with specified attributes from a given query, ensuring that the query and the generated image are distinguishable. To our knowledge, this task has never been explored before. We create a dataset, referred to as MIRFashionEV, comprising 40,000 fashion images with 10 distinct attributes and 1,600,000 generated images. We standardize fashion attribute manipulation and propose a neural rendering pipeline to enable mass deployment. In addition, we introduce an innovative evaluation metric to tackle the query uniqueness challenge. Our experiments aim to provide insights into the characteristics of the MIRFashionEV dataset and the efficacy of the retrieval methods.

the underdetermined equation $Ax=y$ where $A$ is a bounded linear operator mapping a Banach space to a Hilbert space, and $\R$ is a strongly convex function defined in that space, is considered for cases of incomplete data and noisy input. A dual gradient approach, though suffering from semi-convergence, can approximate the $\R$-optimal solution. Its performance has consistent results when input data is noisy, and even under the presence of sparsity-promoting regularization it delivers consistent results. A key advantage of the method is its under conditions of incoherence and the dimensionality of $A$ being much smaller than the ambient space dimension, achieving linear convergence rate. To further enhance performance, the method incorporates a acceleration technique initially developed for the standard least squares problem. Its integration results in achieving a tenfold acceleration over the native dual gradient method.

We have developed a new evaluation protocol by integrating existing methods and conducting comprehensive analyses on the Lorentzian matching cost, revealing its limitations in handling real-world scenarios. We introduce an accurate matching cost evaluation framework, referred to as LoreMatch, which serves as a gold standard for assessing matching costs. We examined multiple light field depth estimation methods using the LoreMatch metric and found that conventional matching costs may mislead the design of depth estimation algorithms. We propose a cost-effective, learning-based matching cost module, named LoreMatch, which outperforms conventional methods and demonstrates superior performance on the LoreMatch metric while also showing improved robustness to distortion scenarios. However, developing these theories involves a complex task: deriving an action principle that accurately captures their behavior. This technical note utilizes the formulation of double field theory to create action frameworks for these alternative gravity theories. By doing so, it resolves the ambiguities associated with their corresponding motion equations. As a result, this note embeds three theories – Torsional Newton-Cartan gravity, Carrollian gravity, and String Newton-Cartan gravity – within double field theory and derives their respective action frameworks for comparison with previously established literature results.

In this paper, we introduce a new approach to promote energy efficiency in forward error correction through sleep mode, contemporary methods of which often rely on either explicit feedback from error correction or external management systems, which are known to consume a considerable amount of bandwidth and power. In contrast, we devise an application-driven, cross-layer protocol to inform the application of impending error correction during data transmission while maintaining the correction process's independence. The proposed approach is evaluated in two scenarios: one using UDP and the other using TCP, with the results demonstrating a significant reduction in energy consumption of around 17% on average, along with a marked decrease in latency of around 27% on average.
